content: The prevalence of asthma has been increasing in recent years. Epidemiological studies suggest that there is a correlation between the onset of asthma and non-allergic dietary factors, particularly a high-calorie diet. These dietary factors may be considered as additional, potentially significant risk factors for asthma. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of dietary calorie reduction on chronic asthma in both adults and children. To gather relevant data, the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register of trials was searched using predefined terms. Bibliographies of included studies were reviewed, and authors of known studies were contacted to obtain further information about both published and unpublished trials. The most recent search was conducted in May 2006. Randomised-controlled trials that investigated dietary calorie reduction were included in the analysis. Three authors independently assessed each study, and any disagreements were resolved through consensus. The quality of the studies was also independently evaluated. The main results included one trial of moderate methodological quality, which involved 38 patients with chronic asthma. In this trial, significant improvements were observed in lung function parameters, specifically forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and forced vital capacity (FVC), in the group receiving the active dietary intervention compared to the control group. No serious adverse effects related to the dietary interventions were reported. The authors concluded that there is currently very limited evidence regarding the effects of dietary interventions, such as calorie-controlled diets, as part of a comprehensive weight-loss program for asthma management. While these dietary strategies cannot yet be recommended as adjunctive interventions alongside drug-based therapies for asthma, they may offer benefits for certain individual patients. However, the overall impact of a calorie-controlled diet on asthma symptoms and signs in the general population of individuals with asthma remains unclear.
